paragraphs.source_en: Lee (1979) has described the increasing contacts between Bantu groups and the Dobe San. This relationship proceeded rapidly from an initial trading relationship to one in which San people worked as servants on seasonally occupied Tswana cattle-posts. Gradually the Dobe San had begun to accumulate a small herd of goats, partly from their exchange with Bantu or with San servants in Bantu villages.

paragraphs.source_en: A similar pattern cannot be excluded for the Central Saharan foragers. If some groups became pastoralists, it would cause substantial changes not only in their lifestyle but also in their ideology (Goodman 1988). As herders, the mouflon and antelope would no longer be of major importance, but the cattle would occupy the first place in everyday as well as spiritual life. As pastoralists they would socialize with other pastoral groups, mix with them, entering into their culture, and possibly adopting their habits, rituals and ceremonies. With the new lifestyle the newly adapted pastoralists would no longer maintain the beliefs of their huntergatherer ancestors and these beliefs would cease to be represented in the rock art.

paragraphs.source_en: The adoption of a new culture is ethnographically documented. Those San who were moving between two different cultures executed paintings that reflected this cultural split (Jolly 1998). Therefore there are rock paintings illustrating two different rites, one San in form such as a trance dance, and the other Sotho, such as a circumcision rite, both depicted by the same San group. It is common for Mbuti pygmy youths to be initiated with villager youths according to the custom of the villagers, and Okiek Dorobo sometimes send their children to neighbouring Masai settlements to take part in initiation ceremonies (Jolly 1998). There are many examples of hunter gatherers almost totally adopting the rites and beliefs of neighbouring peoples.
